The two resulting centrosomes become the two poles of the mitotic spindle, which is why centriole number is guarded so carefully: extra centrosomes cause multipolar divisions and chromosome missegregation, and they are common in tumors.

The centrosome is not the only organizer, and in many cell types it is not even the main one. Differentiated epithelial cells release microtubule minus ends and re-anchor them at apical sites, building parallel arrays that run top to bottom. Neurons nucleate microtubules at the centrosome only early in development, then rely on Golgi outposts, augmin-dependent branching from existing microtubules, and severing enzymes to populate axons and dendrites. Skeletal muscle anchors microtubules at the nuclear envelope. Higher plants have no centrosome at all: their cortical microtubules are nucleated in dispersed fashion along the cell periphery and, remarkably, self-organize into ordered arrays that steer cellulose deposition and hence plant cell shape.

Minus ends, long thought inert, have their own dedicated protein family: CAMSAPs in animals bind and stabilize free minus ends, allowing non-centrosomal arrays to persist. Severing enzymes — katanin, spastin and fidgetin — cut microtubules along their length using AAA-ATPase machinery, seeding new arrays from fragments; mutations in spastin are a leading cause of hereditary spastic paraplegia, an axon-degenerating disease.

The principle to keep is that geometry is destiny. By choosing where nucleation templates and minus-end anchors sit, a cell converts one polymer chemistry into radial asters, parallel rails, cortical hoops or a bipolar spindle — whichever architecture the moment requires.

sections.heading: Kinesins and Dyneins: The Motors that Walk on Microtubules
sections.body:
Diffusion is fast across a bacterium and hopeless across a neuron. A synaptic vesicle diffusing freely would take years to travel a meter-long axon; real cargo makes the trip in days. The difference is made by motor proteins that burn ATP to walk along microtubules: the kinesins, which mostly move toward plus ends and thus outward from the cell center, and the dyneins, which move toward minus ends and thus inward. Between them they run the cell's entire long-haul logistics network.

Conventional kinesin, now kinesin-1, was discovered in 1985 by Ron Vale, Thomas Reese and Michael Sheetz in extruded axoplasm from the squid giant axon, a preparation in which organelle traffic continues in a dish. The molecule is a dimer: two motor heads joined through a coiled-coil stalk to tails that bind cargo adapters. It walks hand over hand, each 16-nanometer swing of a head advancing the molecule's center by exactly 8 nanometers — one tubulin dimer — per ATP hydrolyzed. The two heads coordinate through tension in the short neck linkers so that one stays bound while the other steps, letting a single kinesin take a hundred or more steps before letting go. Optical trap experiments show one molecule stalls at a load of about 6 piconewtons, and moves at roughly 0.5 to 1 micrometer per second unloaded. The human genome encodes about 45 kinesins in 14 families; most are plus-end-directed transporters, but kinesin-14s walk minus-ward and kinesin-13s do not walk at all, serving instead as depolymerases.

Cytoplasmic dynein is a different kind of machine altogether: enormous, ancient and singular. One dynein heavy chain exceeds 500 kilodaltons, and the working motor — two heavy chains plus a retinue of intermediate and light chains — approaches 1.5 megadaltons. Its engine is a ring of six AAA+ ATPase modules; ATP turnover in the ring swings a slender stalk whose tip grips the microtubule, and a buttress and linker convert the ring's motions into steps that are larger and more variable than kinesin's. Alone, mammalian dynein shuffles weakly; to run processively it must join the dynactin complex, whose backbone is a short actin-like Arp1 filament, together with a coiled-coil cargo adapter such as BicD2 or Hook3. This tripartite assembly is the cell's principal inward hauler, carrying endosomes, autophagosomes, viruses, mRNAs and signaling endosomes from axon tips back to the cell body — a route exploited, infamously, by herpesviruses and rabies.

Most cargoes carry both motor types at once, and their tug-of-war, biased by adapters, phosphorylation and the tubulin code on the rails beneath, decides net direction. Fast axonal transport runs outbound at up to about 400 millimeters per day; slower classes move cytoskeletal proteins at a millimeter a day. Mitochondria pause and reverse under local calcium control so they accumulate where work is being done.

When the railway fails, neurons fail first, because their distances are longest. Mutations in KIF5A cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and ALS; mutations in dynein and its adapter BICD2 cause spinal muscular atrophy variants; kinesin and dynein defects at the ciliary base cause the transport diseases of the next sections. Kinesin-5 inhibitors have been tested as antimitotic cancer drugs, aiming at the spindle motor rather than at tubulin itself.

sections.heading: The Mitotic Spindle: Microtubules Divide the Genome
sections.body:
Every division of a human cell must deal 46 chromosomes into two exactly equal hands. The machine that does it, the mitotic spindle, is built almost entirely from microtubules and motors, assembled in minutes, used once and dismantled. Its performance is extraordinary: a healthy cell missegregates a chromosome perhaps once in a hundred divisions or less, and the checkpoint that guards the process can hold the entire cell hostage to a single unattached chromosome.

Spindle assembly begins when the duplicated centrosomes separate, driven apart along the nuclear surface by the plus-end motor kinesin-5, which cross-links antiparallel microtubules and slides them outward. At the same time, phosphorylation by mitotic kinases makes the microtubule population roughly ten times more dynamic, so each centrosome becomes a furious aster of probing plus ends. When the nuclear envelope breaks down, the asters invade the chromosome space and the search begins. Chromosomes are not passive: a gradient of the GTPase Ran around chromatin locally releases spindle assembly factors, and the augmin complex nucleates new microtubules from the sides of existing ones, thickening the forming spindle from within. Egg extracts can build a spindle with no centrosomes at all, proof that the structure is a self-organizing system rather than a machine bolted to two hubs.

The critical connections are made at kinetochores, layered protein complexes, roughly 200 nanometers across in humans, built on the centromere of each chromosome. Each human kinetochore binds a fiber of about 15 to 25 microtubules. The outer plate's NDC80 complexes grip the microtubule lattice in a way that holds tighter under tension yet still allows the fiber's plus ends, buried in the kinetochore, to grow and shrink while attached. Sister kinetochores must attach to opposite poles — biorientation. Wrong attachments happen constantly and are corrected: the kinase Aurora B, sitting at the inner centromere, phosphorylates and loosens grips that are not under proper tension, releasing errors for another try while sparing correct, tension-bearing attachments.

Until every kinetochore is properly attached, the spindle assembly checkpoint broadcasts a wait signal: unattached kinetochores catalyze production of an inhibitor that blocks the anaphase-promoting complex, APC/C. The instant the last kinetochore is captured, inhibitor production ceases, APC/C fires, and the protease separase is unleashed to cut the cohesin rings that have held sister chromatids together since replication. Anaphase follows in two movements. In anaphase A, kinetochore fibers shorten, depolymerizing at both ends while the kinetochore holds on, reeling chromosomes toward the poles. In anaphase B, motors sliding the interpolar overlap apart, plus cortical dynein pulling on astral microtubules, push and haul the poles themselves away from each other.

The spindle then hands off to actin. Signals from the central overlap zone position an actin and myosin II contractile ring at the equator, which constricts the membrane through the former spindle midline; the last microtubule stub, the midbody, marks the point of final cutting, or abscission. Two complete genomes, two centrosomes, two cells.

The spindle's medical importance is direct: it is the target of the taxanes and vinca alkaloids described later, which kill dividing tumor cells by jamming spindle microtubule dynamics and tripping the checkpoint until the cell dies or exits division catastrophically.

sections.heading: Cilia and Flagella: The 9+2 Axoneme and Intraflagellar Transport
sections.body:
Long before there were microscopists, cells were rowing. Cilia and flagella — the terms overlap; eukaryotic flagella are simply long cilia — are membrane-wrapped beating rods built on a microtubule core called the axoneme, and their architecture has been conserved for over a billion years, essentially identical in the green alga Chlamydomonas, the protist Paramecium, and the human airway. A cross-section shows the most famous arrangement in cell biology: nine doublet microtubules in a ring around a central pair of singlets, the 9+2 axoneme, about 250 nanometers in diameter and typically 5 to 10 micrometers long, though sperm flagella reach 50.

Each outer doublet is a complete 13-protofilament A-tubule with an incomplete 10-protofilament B-tubule fused to its side. Rows of axonemal dynein motors are mounted permanently along each A-tubule, their heads reaching across to walk on the neighboring doublet's B-tubule. Because all nine doublets are anchored together at the base and tied to their neighbors by elastic nexin links, the dyneins' sliding cannot proceed freely; constrained sliding becomes bending. Radial spokes and the central pair apparatus act as a distributor, activating dynein on one side of the ring while quieting the other, and switching sides rhythmically, which converts a static push into a propagating wave. Airway cilia beat around 10 to 20 times per second; coordinated fields of them move the mucus escalator that clears the lungs of inhaled debris.

Every cilium grows from a basal body, a centriole that has docked at the plasma membrane; its nine triplets seed the nine doublets. Growth poses a logistics problem: the axoneme assembles at its distal tip, yet the cilium contains no ribosomes. The solution, discovered in Chlamydomonas in 1993 by Keith Kozminski and Joel Rosenbaum, is intraflagellar transport, or IFT: trains of protein carriers shuttle along the doublets, outbound under kinesin-2 with fresh tubulin and parts, inbound under a dedicated IFT dynein with turnover products. Shut off IFT and the cilium shortens and disappears; the organelle exists in dynamic equilibrium, continuously rebuilt at its tip.

The deepest surprise of modern cell biology is the primary cilium. Most non-dividing vertebrate cells — kidney tubule cells, neurons, chondrocytes, photoreceptors — carry a single, immotile 9+0 cilium lacking the central pair and dynein arms. It is not a fossil; it is an antenna. The Hedgehog signaling pathway, which patterns the embryonic limb and neural tube, works by shuttling its receptors and effectors through the primary cilium; polycystin channels in kidney cilia monitor the tubule environment; the photoreceptor outer segment, where vision begins, is an elaborated cilium through which all its protein traffic must pass.

Disease follows the anatomy. Defects in motile cilia cause primary ciliary dyskinesia: immotile airway cilia bring chronic sinus and lung infection, immotile sperm bring infertility, and, because nodal cilia set the embryo's left-right axis by driving a directional fluid flow, about half of affected people have situs inversus — a mirror-imaged body, the combination known as Kartagener syndrome. Defects in primary cilia and IFT cause the ciliopathies: polycystic kidney disease, one of the commonest inherited disorders, along with Bardet-Biedl and Joubert syndromes, retinal degeneration and some forms of obesity and skeletal dysplasia. One conserved organelle, dozens of diseases: anatomy is destiny again.

sections.heading: Intermediate Filaments: Keratins, Vimentin, Neurofilaments and Lamins
sections.body:
The third filament system is the least famous and the toughest. Intermediate filaments, about 10 nanometers across, were named for a diameter between actin's and the thick myosin filaments of muscle where they were first noticed. They differ from actin and microtubules in almost every design decision, and the differences all point one way: these are tension-bearing ropes, not dynamic engines.

The subunit is not a compact globule but an elongated rod: a central alpha-helical domain of around 310 residues flanked by variable head and tail domains. Two subunits twist into a parallel coiled-coil dimer; two dimers align antiparallel and staggered into a tetramer; eight tetramers bundle into a unit-length filament that anneals end to end with others and then compacts into the mature 10-nanometer rope. Because the tetramer is antiparallel, the finished filament has no polarity — no plus or minus end — and therefore no motors walk on it and no treadmilling occurs. The subunits bind no nucleotide; assembly costs no ATP or GTP. Exchange happens along the length as well as at ends, and is controlled largely by phosphorylation, which drives disassembly, most dramatically when the nuclear lamina is dissolved at the start of mitosis.

Mechanically, intermediate filaments are the opposite of microtubules: flexible, with a persistence length under a micrometer, but almost unbreakable, stretching to two or three times their resting length and stiffening as they extend. Networks of them behave like a safety harness — compliant in ordinary life, rigid under crisis loads. A cell pulled or sheared beyond what actin can absorb hangs its survival on this system.

Unlike actin and tubulin, intermediate filament proteins are a large differentiated family, about 70 genes in humans, expressed by tissue. Types I and II are the keratins, over 50 genes, always assembling as acidic-basic heterodimers: epithelial keratins form the dense cytoplasmic web of skin, gut and airway lining, and specialized hard keratins build hair and nails. Type III includes vimentin in fibroblasts and white blood cells, desmin forming the lateral scaffold that keeps muscle sarcomeres in register, and GFAP in astrocytes. Type IV, the neurofilaments, fill axons; their spacing, set by long side-arm tails, is a major determinant of axon caliber and hence conduction speed. Pathologists exploit this tissue registry daily, typing metastatic tumors of unknown origin by which intermediate filament they express.

Type V is different in kind: the nuclear lamins, the family's ancestors, form a meshwork lining the inner nuclear membrane that shapes and protects the nucleus, tethers chromatin, and disassembles and reforms at each mitosis under CDK1 phosphorylation. Every animal cell has lamins; cytoplasmic intermediate filaments are, evolutionarily, their descendants that moved out.

The system's importance is written in its diseases. In epidermolysis bullosa simplex, point mutations in keratin 5 or 14 make basal skin cells shear apart at trivial friction, blistering from birth. Desmin mutations cause cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy; neurofilament mutations cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy; GFAP mutations cause the leukodystrophy called Alexander disease. Mutations in lamin A produce an astonishing spread of disorders — Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, lipodystrophy, and Hutchinson-Gilford progeria, in which a cryptic splice site yields a permanently membrane-anchored fragment, progerin, and children age with terrible speed. Ropes fail rarely, but when they fail, whole tissues feel it.

sections.heading: Linking the Networks: Cross-Talk, Junctions and Mechanics
sections.body:
Textbooks separate the three filament systems; cells do not. Every large-scale behavior — dividing, crawling, resisting a stretch, holding an epithelium together — is a joint production, and a family of dedicated linker proteins plus shared signaling keeps the systems coordinated.

The professional connectors are the plakins, giant proteins with binding sites for more than one filament type. Plectin, at over 500 kilodaltons, ties intermediate filaments to actin, to microtubules and to membrane junctions; mutations cause epidermolysis bullosa with muscular dystrophy, skin and muscle failing together. Another plakin, called ACF7 or MACF1, guides growing microtubule plus ends along actin bundles toward the cell edge, so the highways get laid where protrusion is happening. The spectraplakin family in flies performs the same marriage, and losing it disorganizes both networks at once.

Epithelia display the division of labor most clearly at their junctions. Adherens junctions couple the actin belts of neighboring cells through cadherins, letting a sheet contract as a unit — the mechanism that bends flat epithelium into tubes during development. Desmosomes, built on desmosomal cadherins and plakoglobin and desmoplakin, rivet the intermediate filament networks of neighbors into one tissue-spanning web; hemidesmosomes do the same downward, tying keratin to the basement membrane through integrin alpha-6 beta-4. The result is a composite material: actin supplies adjustable tension, keratin supplies tear resistance, and the junctions make a thousand cells mechanically one. Autoimmune attack on desmosomes, in pemphigus, makes skin cells simply let go of each other.

Directed cell migration shows the cross-talk in time as well as space. The microtubule system, oriented by the centrosome and by cortical capture sites, defines front and back, delivering Rac activators to the leading edge and relaxing adhesion at the rear; the actin system executes protrusion and contraction; the vimentin network reorganizes to template long-lived protrusions and stiffen the trailing cell body. Drugs that kill microtubules do not stop actin from making lamellipodia, but the cell loses persistence and wanders — steering without the map.

Mechanics runs the other way too: forces reshape signaling. Focal adhesions grow when pulled, because talin unfolds under piconewton loads and exposes cryptic binding sites for vinculin — a genuine molecular force sensor. The transcription regulators YAP and TAZ read cytoskeletal tension and substrate stiffness and translate them into growth decisions; mesenchymal stem cells cultured on soft, brain-like gels tend toward neurons, on stiff, bone-like substrates toward osteoblasts, with actomyosin contractility as the measuring instrument. The nucleus itself is wired into the system: the LINC complex, SUN and nesprin proteins spanning the nuclear envelope, connects the lamina inside to actin, microtubules and intermediate filaments outside, so a tug on the cell surface arrives at chromatin within milliseconds — faster than any chemical messenger.

Even pathogens respect the integration. Listeria rides actin comets from cell to cell; vaccinia virus surfs actin tails off the cell surface; herpesviruses ride dynein inbound to the nucleus and kinesin outbound; enteropathogenic E. coli remodels the host's actin into a pedestal beneath itself. The cytoskeleton, in short, is one machine with three kinds of moving part, and the linkers are as essential as the filaments.

sections.heading: Drugs, Toxins and Diseases: Breaking the Cytoskeleton on Purpose and by Accident
sections.body:
Much of what is known about the cytoskeleton was learned by poisoning it, and several of the poisons became medicines. Because the filaments are assembled from soluble pools, a small molecule that shifts the assembly balance can transform cell behavior in minutes, making cytoskeletal drugs both superb laboratory tools and potent chemotherapy.

The microtubule drugs fall into two camps. Destabilizers block polymerization or promote disassembly: colchicine, from the autumn crocus, binds tubulin dimers and has been used against gout since antiquity; the vinca alkaloids vincristine and vinblastine, from the Madagascar periwinkle, cap microtubule ends and depolymerize spindles, and remain frontline drugs against leukemias and lymphomas; nocodazole does the same reversibly and is the standard laboratory tool for erasing the microtubule array. Stabilizers do the opposite: paclitaxel, or Taxol, discovered in the bark of the Pacific yew, binds along the microtubule wall and locks the lattice so that dynamics freeze. Both camps kill dividing cells the same way — a spindle that cannot remodel cannot satisfy the assembly checkpoint, and the arrested cell dies — which is why taxanes treat breast, ovarian and lung cancer. Both also share a signature toxicity, peripheral neuropathy, because long axons depend utterly on microtubule transport. Cells growing without dividing are relatively spared, a selectivity window that oncology has exploited for half a century.

Actin's poisons are laboratory rather than clinical, since heart and muscle make systemic actin drugs intolerable. Cytochalasins, fungal metabolites, cap barbed ends; latrunculins, from Red Sea sponges, sequester monomers and dissolve the network; jasplakinolide stabilizes filaments. Phalloidin, the toxin of the death cap mushroom Amanita phalloides, binds and stabilizes F-actin so specifically that its fluorescent conjugates are the universal stain for imaging actin — though in poisoning it is the mushroom's amatoxins, not phalloidin, that destroy the liver.

Inherited diseases map the systems onto tissues. The intermediate filament disorders were listed earlier: blistering skin from keratin mutations, cardiomyopathy from desmin, neuropathy from neurofilaments, progeria from lamin A. Microtubule-side genetics is equally telling: tubulin mutations cause cortical brain malformations such as lissencephaly, as does loss of the dynein regulator LIS1, because building a cortex requires nuclei to ride microtubules through migrating neurons; spastin and KIF5A mutations degenerate the longest spinal axons in hereditary spastic paraplegia; tau misbehavior defines a family of dementias. On the actin side, mutations in the immune actin regulator WASP cause Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, and nonmuscle myosin heavy chain mutations cause a syndrome of deafness, platelet defects and kidney disease.

Infectious agents complete the catalogue, weaponizing the host cytoskeleton with remarkable precision. Clostridium difficile toxins glucosylate Rho GTPases and collapse the intestinal epithelium's actin; Salmonella injects proteins that trigger ruffling and then reverse it, entering the cell and tidying up afterward; Shigella and Listeria propel themselves with actin comets; viruses from HIV to herpes ride the microtubule railway in both directions.

The pattern across all of it is consistent. Attack dynamics and you stop division and transport; attack the ropes and tissues tear; attack the regulators and the cell loses control of its own shape. Each failure mode is a backhanded description of what the healthy system does all day.
